newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EU, U.S. hit S.Korea over "frugality campaign".
newsitem.headline: EU, U.S. hit S.Korea over "frugality campaign".

text.p: The European Union and the United States on Tuesday attacked South Korea over its "frugality campaign", suggesting the government was breaking global trading rules in a bid to cut imports.

At a meeting of the World Trade Organisation's (WTO) Council for Trade in Goods, officials of the two powers called on Seoul to take a clear public stand on the issue which they said was having a serious effect on exports to the key Asian market.

"We believe that (South) Korea has a responsability to reassure its trading partners that the impression that it is hostile to imports and hesitant about two-way trade is mistaken," the EU's Ian Wilkinson told the Council.

"Recent statements by (South) Korean government officials suggesting that it is a citizen's 'patriotic' duty not to consume imports have reinforced the perception of an anti-import bias in Korea," declared U.S. WTO envoy Andrew Stoler.

The campaign was launched last summer by South Korean President Kim Young-sam in the face of a growing balance of payments deficit, which reached $23.7 billion by the end of 1996, and foreign debts totalling more than $100 billion.

But Seoul officials say the drive, which they insist is run by civic groups and non-governmental organisations, is targeted against all consumption of "luxury goods", which has soared since a banking reform in 1993.

Under the luxury catagory, the South Korean government includes electronic products, home appliances, cosmetics, sports equipment, clothing and cars. Imported foreign alcoholic drinks have also been targeted in the campaign.

South Korea's ambassador Joun Yung-sun told the Council on Tuesday the 1993 reform had generated excessive cash which led to an explosion of consumption. The government itself was not involved in any anti-import campaign, he declared.

Trade sources quoted him as saying it was "unfair and unacceptable" for the EU and the United States to imply that officials were encouraging a drive against foreign goods. "I clearly deny such allegations," he added.

EU and U.S. diplomats argue that government complicity is illustrated in what they say has been a mounting number of cases of "administrative harassment" by customs and other authorities against imports and owners of imported goods, especially cars.
Stoler told the Council that other WTO members were sympathetic to South Korea's balance of payment problems.

"However, the arbitrary use of standards, documentation requirements, customs delays, regulatory and labelling requirements, tax audits, or other measures to deter imports not only conflicts with WTO principles and obligations, but would be counter-productive to the competitiveness of the (South) Korean economy over the long run."
Wilkinson said South Korean public officials at all levels were making statements "which are clearly intended to blame imported consumer goods for (South) Korea's current account deficit."
A study of the deficit's structure, he told the Council, "shows this to be utterly false."

"Since all WTO members benefit from an open, equitable and non-discriminatory multilateral trading system, and have a responsability to defend it, a clear public statement from the (South) Korean government disowning all anti-import aspects of the civic "frugality" campaign is now necessary to dispel doubts about Korea's commitment to respect in full its WTO obligations," the EU envoy said.
